difficultyReason: Both speakers accept the premise that animal testing has produced medical benefits and both grant that alternatives are improving; the disagreement is specifically about whether the current benefits justify continuing the practice. Trap (A) is an agreement in disguise; trap (E) shifts to a claim only Farooq addresses.
stimulus: Farooq: Animal testing has unquestionably delivered important medical advances, and I would not deny that. But we now have cell-culture and computational methods that approximate many of those results, and continuing to subject animals to painful trials when those alternatives exist is no longer defensible. Hollister: The alternatives you cite are promising but remain unreliable for many systemic effects. Until that changes, the medical gains from animal studies still outweigh the welfare costs, even granting that those costs are real.
questionStem: Farooq and Hollister disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: animal testing has historically contributed to medical progress

choices.label: B
choices.text: the current welfare costs of animal testing are outweighed by its medical benefits

choices.label: C
choices.text: cell-culture methods will eventually supplant animal testing entirely

choices.label: D
choices.text: subjecting laboratory animals to painful procedures causes genuine harm

choices.label: E
choices.text: regulators have been too slow to approve computational alternatives

explanations.correct: Farooq says the practice is no longer defensible given that alternatives exist; Hollister says the medical gains still outweigh the welfare costs. That is a direct disagreement about the current cost-benefit balance.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Farooq explicitly grants that animal testing has delivered important advances, and Hollister presupposes the same.
explanations.C: Neither speaker addresses complete replacement; both only compare current reliability.
explanations.D: Both would accept that the welfare costs are real; Hollister even concedes this explicitly.
explanations.E: Only Farooq gestures toward the availability of alternatives, and neither speaker takes a position on regulatory pace.

difficultyReason: Both speakers grant that standardized tests correlate with later outcomes and both acknowledge that the correlation is imperfect; the disagreement is specifically over whether the tests should be used as admissions gatekeepers. Trap (D) is a point only one speaker addresses.
stimulus: Ramsey: Standardized admissions tests correlate with first-year college grades, but the correlation is modest and the tests also track family income closely. Given that, we should not let these scores function as gatekeepers for admission. Okafor: The correlation with grades, while imperfect, is still the best single predictor we have, and no admissions office I know of uses the scores as a sole criterion. They belong in the mix precisely because they add information that transcripts alone do not.
questionStem: Ramsey and Okafor's statements most strongly support the claim that they disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: standardized admissions test scores are perfectly correlated with first-year college grades

choices.label: B
choices.text: admissions offices currently use standardized test scores as the sole basis for admission

choices.label: C
choices.text: standardized test scores should be used as a factor in college admissions decisions

choices.label: D
choices.text: transcripts alone are sufficient to predict first-year college grades

choices.label: E
choices.text: standardized test scores correlate with the family income of test-takers

explanations.correct: Ramsey denies the tests should function as gatekeepers; Okafor affirms that they belong in the admissions mix. That is a disagreement about whether the scores should be a factor in admissions.
explanations.A: Both would deny this — Ramsey calls the correlation modest and Okafor calls it imperfect.
explanations.B: Only Okafor addresses current practice; Ramsey takes no position on what offices actually do.
explanations.D: Only Okafor implies transcripts alone are insufficient; Ramsey says nothing about transcripts.
explanations.E: Agreement in disguise — Ramsey asserts this and Okafor does not contest it.

difficultyReason: Both speakers grant that training data includes copyrighted work and both concede the outputs are often novel; the disagreement turns on whether the training itself constitutes infringement. Trap (A) is a factual point both accept; trap (E) shifts to a normative claim only one addresses.
stimulus: Dex: AI image models are trained on vast archives of copyrighted artwork without the artists' consent. Even when the resulting images look nothing like any single source, the training itself is a use of the works, and that use is an infringement. Vera: The training process analyzes statistical features of the images, not the images themselves, and the outputs are typically novel. Reading a book to learn a writing style is not infringement; training on images to learn visual style is analogous.
questionStem: Dex and Vera disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: AI image models are trained on archives that include copyrighted work

choices.label: B
choices.text: the images generated by AI models are typically copies of specific source artworks

choices.label: C
choices.text: training an AI image model on copyrighted artwork constitutes copyright infringement

choices.label: D
choices.text: reading a copyrighted book to study the author's style constitutes infringement

choices.label: E
choices.text: artists should be compensated when their work is used to train AI image models

explanations.correct: Dex says the training itself is infringement; Vera's analogy is meant to show that such training is not infringement. They take opposite positions on exactly this proposition.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers presuppose that copyrighted works are included in the training data.
explanations.B: Both would deny this — Dex says the outputs look nothing like any single source and Vera says outputs are typically novel.
explanations.D: Only Vera addresses the book analogy; Dex does not commit to a position on reading books.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses compensation; the debate is about the legal/conceptual status of training, not about remedy.

difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that some offset projects fail to deliver the promised carbon reductions and both accept that emissions reduction at the source is desirable. The disagreement concerns whether a well-designed offset program can meaningfully substitute for on-site reductions. Trap (B) is an agreement.
stimulus: Mendez: Independent audits have repeatedly found that many forest-based carbon offset projects overstate their actual carbon reductions, sometimes by an order of magnitude. A company buying such offsets instead of cutting its own emissions is not genuinely addressing its climate impact. Halligan: Audit failures have certainly tarnished offset markets, but the problem is poor measurement, not the concept. With rigorous monitoring and verification, a well-designed offset program can achieve real reductions that firms could not practically achieve on-site.
questionStem: Mendez and Halligan disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: forest-based offset projects have sometimes overstated their carbon reductions

choices.label: B
choices.text: reducing emissions at the source is, in principle, a desirable goal

choices.label: C
choices.text: a well-designed offset program can substitute for a company's on-site emissions reductions

choices.label: D
choices.text: current verification protocols are adequate to detect overstated reductions

choices.label: E
choices.text: companies have a legal obligation to purchase carbon offsets

explanations.correct: Mendez claims that buying offsets instead of cutting emissions is not genuinely addressing climate impact; Halligan claims a well-designed offset program can achieve real reductions firms cannot practically make on-site. They disagree about whether offsets can substitute for on-site cuts.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Halligan concedes that audit failures have occurred.
explanations.B: Both accept this; Mendez frames cutting one's own emissions as the genuine response, and Halligan does not deny its desirability.
explanations.D: Only Mendez alludes to audit findings; neither takes a position on whether current protocols are adequate in general.
explanations.E: Legal obligation is out of scope — neither speaker mentions any legal requirement.

difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that antibiotic resistance is rising and both accept that over-prescription contributes. The disagreement turns on where the primary responsibility for reform should fall. Trap (A) is a shared premise; trap (E) splits the speakers the wrong way.
stimulus: Dr. Bae: Antibiotic resistance is rising, and over-prescription in primary care is a major driver. The most effective lever is stricter prescribing guidelines enforced at the clinical level, where individual prescribing decisions actually get made. Dr. Ilundain: Physician-level guidelines alone will not be enough. The bulk of antibiotic use is in livestock agriculture, not human medicine, and regulating agricultural use is where reform will make the biggest difference.
questionStem: On the basis of their statements, Dr. Bae and Dr. Ilundain are committed to disagreeing about which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotic resistance in humans is a growing problem.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Primary-care physicians sometimes prescribe antibiotics when they are not clinically warranted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The most effective target for reducing antibiotic resistance is prescribing practices in primary care.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Livestock agriculture accounts for the bulk of antibiotic use.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulation of antibiotic use by farmers would, by itself, solve the problem of antibiotic resistance.

explanations.correct: Dr. Bae says the most effective lever is clinical-level prescribing guidelines; Dr. Ilundain denies this by saying the biggest difference will come from regulating agricultural use. That is a direct disagreement about where the most effective target lies.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers take resistance as a given problem worth addressing.
explanations.B: Only Dr. Bae addresses primary-care prescribing specifically; Dr. Ilundain says nothing about whether individual prescriptions are clinically unwarranted.
explanations.D: Only Dr. Ilundain asserts this; Dr. Bae does not deny it and takes no position on the share.
explanations.E: This splits them the wrong way — Dr. Ilundain says agricultural regulation will make the biggest difference, not that it would solve the problem alone; Dr. Bae does not address it at all.

difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that rent control protects current tenants and that housing supply is strained. The disagreement is specifically about the net effect on renters overall. Trap (B) is a shared premise; trap (D) is a claim only one speaker addresses.
stimulus: Navarro: Rent control protects the tenants who are already in regulated units, and I grant that. But when landlords can't adjust rents on existing stock, developers build fewer new units, and renters who are not yet in the system end up paying more for worse housing. On balance, rent control hurts renters as a group. Sung: Protecting the tenants already in place is not a minor thing — it's the whole point. Displacement is catastrophic for those affected, and a policy that prevents it benefits renters, even if supply effects are real at the margin.
questionStem: Navarro and Sung disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: rent control, taken as a whole, benefits renters as a group

choices.label: B
choices.text: tenants currently living in rent-controlled units are protected by the policy

choices.label: C
choices.text: housing supply effects from rent control are entirely negligible

choices.label: D
choices.text: displacement of tenants imposes severe costs on those affected

choices.label: E
choices.text: developers should be encouraged to build more housing than they currently do

explanations.correct: Navarro concludes that on balance rent control hurts renters as a group; Sung concludes that the policy benefits renters. They take opposite positions on the net effect.
explanations.B: Agreement in disguise — Navarro explicitly grants this and Sung affirms it.
explanations.C: Sung calls supply effects 'real at the margin,' so neither speaker denies the effects exist.
explanations.D: Only Sung characterizes displacement as catastrophic; Navarro does not deny this — he simply doesn't address it directly.
explanations.E: Neither speaker makes recommendations about developer incentives.

difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that the traditional literary canon is narrow in its demographic origins and both accept that canonical works have literary merit. The disagreement is about whether the curriculum should be reorganized around broader representation. Trap (C) is an agreement; trap (E) splits them the wrong way.
stimulus: Acheampong: The traditional literary canon taught in our universities is overwhelmingly drawn from a narrow slice of authors. That is a fact, and it limits students' sense of what literature can do. A curriculum organized around broader representation would serve students better. Pilsen: The canon is narrow in origin, but the works in it have earned their place through sustained literary power. Reorganizing the curriculum around representation risks replacing one criterion for inclusion with another that has little to do with how good the writing is.
questionStem: Acheampong and Pilsen's statements commit them to disagreeing about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the works in the traditional literary canon possess any literary merit

choices.label: B
choices.text: the university literature curriculum should be reorganized to emphasize broader authorial representation

choices.label: C
choices.text: the traditional literary canon is drawn from a narrow demographic range

choices.label: D
choices.text: literary merit is a criterion that can be applied objectively

choices.label: E
choices.text: students currently have an accurate sense of what literature can do

explanations.correct: Acheampong endorses a curriculum reorganized around broader representation; Pilsen opposes reorganizing on those grounds. They take directly opposing positions on the reorganization proposal.
explanations.A: Neither speaker denies the canon has literary merit — Pilsen affirms it and Acheampong does not deny it.
explanations.C: Agreement in disguise — both speakers grant the canon's narrow origin.
explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses objectivity of merit directly.
explanations.E: Only Acheampong claims students' sense is limited; Pilsen does not affirm that students currently have an accurate sense — he just doesn't address it.

difficultyReason: Both speakers grant that juries historically have engaged in nullification and both accept that judges instruct juries to apply the law. The disagreement is about whether jurors have a legitimate right to nullify, not whether they are able to or whether it happens. Trap (A) is an agreement.
stimulus: Yusuf: A jury's power to acquit against the evidence — so-called nullification — has been exercised throughout the history of common law. When a jury's conscience tells it a conviction under a particular statute would be unjust, the jury is entitled to refuse to convict, regardless of the judge's instructions. Leclerc: Jurors have the raw power to acquit against the evidence, and no one disputes that juries have done so. But a power is not a right. The law binds the juror just as it binds the judge, and exercising nullification violates the oath the juror has taken.
questionStem: Yusuf and Leclerc disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: juries have historically acquitted defendants against the weight of the evidence

choices.label: B
choices.text: a juror is entitled to refuse to convict when the juror believes conviction would be unjust

choices.label: C
choices.text: judges instruct juries to apply the law as given

choices.label: D
choices.text: a juror who nullifies can be legally punished for doing so

choices.label: E
choices.text: nullification has ever produced a just outcome in a particular case

explanations.correct: Yusuf says the juror is entitled to refuse to convict when conscience so dictates; Leclerc denies this entitlement, distinguishing raw power from right. That is exactly their point of disagreement.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Leclerc concedes that no one disputes juries have done this.
explanations.C: Both accept this as background; neither disputes it.
explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses punishment of nullifying jurors.
explanations.E: Neither speaker takes a position on the outcomes of particular historical cases.

difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that reenactments engage the public and that they involve simplification. The disagreement is specifically about whether simplification for engagement produces a net educational gain. Trap (C) is an agreement; trap (E) is a point only one speaker addresses.
stimulus: Professor Okonkwo: Historical reenactments draw large audiences and generate interest in the past, and I grant that this engagement is valuable. But reenactors simplify and sanitize the events they stage, and audiences walk away with tidier versions of history than the record supports. The net educational effect is negative. Curator Holst: Reenactors do simplify — they must, to stage anything at all. But an oversimplified encounter that leaves a visitor curious enough to read further is a net gain over no encounter at all.
questionStem: Professor Okonkwo and Curator Holst disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: historical reenactments tend to draw large audiences

choices.label: B
choices.text: historical reenactments, on balance, have a positive educational effect on their audiences

choices.label: C
choices.text: reenactors simplify the events they stage

choices.label: D
choices.text: the historical record of the events reenactors stage is well-documented

choices.label: E
choices.text: audiences of reenactments sometimes read further about the events afterward

explanations.correct: Okonkwo concludes that the net educational effect is negative; Holst concludes that the result is a net gain. They disagree squarely on the net educational effect.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Okonkwo asserts this and Holst does not contest it.
explanations.C: Agreement in disguise — both speakers affirm that simplification occurs.
explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses the state of the historical record.
explanations.E: Only Holst mentions post-reenactment reading; Okonkwo does not deny it happens.

difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that a universal basic income would relieve acute poverty and both accept that it is costly. The disagreement concerns whether the work-disincentive concern should block the policy. Trap (A) is an agreement; trap (D) splits the speakers the wrong way.
stimulus: Patel: A universal basic income would dramatically reduce acute poverty, and the pilot programs we have seen bear this out. The main objection — that recipients would stop working — has not materialized in any rigorous study. We should not let an empirically unsupported worry block a policy with documented benefits. Reyna: The pilots have indeed shown little aggregate decline in work effort. I concede that. But pilots are temporary, and people behave differently when they know a benefit is permanent. The work-disincentive concern is not refuted by short-run pilots; it just hasn't been properly tested yet.
questionStem: Patel and Reyna disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: universal basic income pilot programs have reduced poverty among participants

choices.label: B
choices.text: the existing evidence about pilots is sufficient to set aside the work-disincentive concern

choices.label: C
choices.text: pilot participants in universal basic income studies showed significant aggregate declines in work effort

choices.label: D
choices.text: people behave identically whether a benefit is temporary or permanent

choices.label: E
choices.text: a universal basic income would eliminate poverty entirely

explanations.correct: Patel says the empirically unsupported worry should not block the policy — i.e., current evidence suffices to set the concern aside. Reyna says the concern is not refuted by short-run pilots, meaning the evidence does not suffice. That is their exact point of disagreement.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Patel asserts poverty reduction and Reyna does not contest it.
explanations.C: Agreement in disguise — Reyna concedes that pilots showed little aggregate decline, and Patel asserts the same.
explanations.D: This splits them the wrong way — Patel does not commit to the 'identically' claim; his point is that the empirical evidence should carry weight. Reyna rejects identity of behavior, but Patel never affirms it.
explanations.E: Neither speaker claims UBI would eliminate poverty entirely; Patel says only that it would dramatically reduce acute poverty.
